description: A one-line if and else that produces a value, and when not to use it.

content.title: Anatomy of a ternary
content.caption: It is called **ternary** because it takes three parts. It is the only Java operator that does.

items.title: if and else
items.text: Fine, but long just to choose one word.

items.title: Ternary
items.text: Condition `?` value if true `:` value if false.

content.value: A ternary is an **expression**: it produces a value, so you must use it. `marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";` on its own is a compile error. Assign it or print it.

content.question: What is stored in `r` when `age` is `12`?
content.explain: `12 >= 18` is false, so the value after the `:` is chosen.

content.value: A ternary shines inside a print, where an `if` and `else` would need four extra lines to pick one word.

steps.note: `count == 1` is true, so it picks `" item"`.
`count == 1` is false, so it picks `" items"`.

content.title: Picking a word, picking a number
content.outro: Keep the brackets round a ternary inside a print. Without them, `+` joins the text before the `?` is reached.

content.caption: Any type works, numbers, `char`, `boolean`, text, as long as both sides give the **same** type.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `60 >= 75` is false, so the value after `:` is chosen.

items.sub: If the branches do real work, like several prints, use `if` and `else`.
A ternary inside a ternary is legal, and almost unreadable.

content.question: You need to pick one of four messages. What fits best?
options: An else if chain or a switch
content.explain: A ternary chooses between exactly two values. Three or more alternatives belong in a chain or a switch.

content.title: Four ways to decide

quiz.question: What are the three parts of a ternary, in order?
options: The condition, the value if true, the value if false
The value if true, the condition, the value if false
quiz.explain: `condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse`. The `?` separates the question from the answers and the `:` separates the two answers.

quiz.question: What does `int price = age < 13 ? 120 : 250;` store when age is 30?
quiz.explain: The condition is false for 30, so the value after the `:` is chosen.

quiz.question: Why is `marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";` on its own a compile error?
options: A ternary produces a value, and that value has to be used.
A ternary cannot be used with text.
It needs an `if` in front of it.
quiz.explain: It is an expression, not an instruction. Assign it to a variable or print it, so the answer has somewhere to go.

quiz.question: Why do you need brackets in `"Total: " + (a > b ? a : b)`?
options: Without them the `+` would join the text before the ternary is reached.
quiz.explain: `+` binds more tightly than `?`, so without brackets Java would build a piece of text first and the condition would no longer be comparing what you meant.

quiz.question: When should you NOT use a ternary?
options: When the branches do real work, or when there are three or more alternatives
When choosing a word inside a print
quiz.explain: The ternary is for choosing one of two values. Work belongs in `if` and `else`, and several alternatives belong in a chain or a switch.
